variants.label: Intact Ac
variants.explanation: Ac encodes its transposase and is autonomous.

variants.label: Ds alone
variants.explanation: This representative Ds cannot supply transposase.

variants.label: Ds with Ac
variants.explanation: Compatible Ac protein can support movement. Ds remains non-autonomous.

exercise.question: Ds moves when Ac protein is supplied. What is Ds?
exercise.explanation: Supplying protein changes mobility conditions, not the genetic capacity encoded by Ds.

check.question: Does an intact transposase gene guarantee an insertion now?
options: No: compatible ends, protein activity and host conditions also matter
check.explanation: Autonomy describes capacity, not a guaranteed event.

variants.label: Maize observations
variants.explanation: Genetic and cytological observations supported the controlling-element interpretation; this is not a reconstructed experiment.

variants.label: Ac absent
variants.explanation: The selected Ds cannot undergo Ac-dependent movement without compatible transposase.

variants.label: Ac present
variants.explanation: Movement becomes possible, not certain.

exercise.question: Remove Ac and every other compatible transposase source. Predict Ds mobility.
exercise.explanation: The selected Ds cannot encode functional transposase.

check.question: Why qualify claims about Ds?
options: Different Ds derivatives have different structures
check.explanation: A single schematic cannot explain every Ds-associated chromosome or phenotype outcome.

variants.label: Boundaries
variants.explanation: The outer TSDs are host-derived. Opposing terminal arrows represent inverted end motifs.

variants.label: Genes
variants.explanation: Coding arrows show schematic orientation; cargo and transposase have different roles.

variants.label: Insertion junction
variants.explanation: Both TSD copies trace to one target site, not two elements.

exercise.question: Which regions move as part of this element?
exercise.explanation: TIRs lie inside element boundaries; TSDs lie outside.

check.question: Two flanking direct host repeats demonstrate what?
check.explanation: Count complete elements independently of the target repeats.

variants.label: Ty: Class I
variants.explanation: Yeast Ty provides an experimentally supported RNA-intermediate example.

variants.label: Tn5: Class II
variants.explanation: The selected conservative pathway relocates one element.

variants.label: Tn3: Class II
variants.explanation: A DNA-based pathway can increase element copy number.

exercise.question: An element uses RNA followed by reverse transcription. Classify it.
options: Class II because its product is DNA
exercise.explanation: The intermediate and reverse-transcription step identify Class I.

check.question: Does DNA-based movement always require conservative excision?
check.explanation: Tn3 is a counterexample to a universal cut-and-paste claim.

variants.label: Tn5
variants.explanation: One copy overall, with target-side 9 bp TSDs; donor repair is unresolved.

variants.label: Tn3 cointegrate
variants.explanation: Replication creates two directly oriented copies in one circle.

variants.label: Tn3 resolution
variants.explanation: Two copies remain; target-side 5 bp TSDs persist. Physical unlinking is not calculated.

exercise.question: One circle contains both backbones and two direct Tn3 copies. What occurred?
exercise.explanation: The selected replicative transition joins backbones and increases copy number.

check.question: How many Tn3 copies remain after resolution?
check.explanation: Resolution does not reverse replication.

variants.label: IS10
variants.explanation: Simplified IS10 architecture; regulatory and possible overlapping coding details are omitted.

variants.label: Composite comparison
variants.explanation: Cargo bracketed by IS modules is a composite architecture, not a single simple IS.

variants.label: Functional asymmetry
variants.explanation: Native Tn10 modules are not functionally equivalent: IS10-R supplies normal movement functions.

exercise.question: Which region directly supplies movement machinery?
exercise.explanation: Resistance cargo has a different function from transposition genes.

check.question: Can one IS diagram establish every IS family’s mechanism?
check.explanation: Coding organization, ends and mechanisms vary.

variants.label: Tn5
variants.explanation: Inverted IS50 modules; this expands anatomy without changing the abstract engine.

variants.label: Tn10
variants.explanation: Inverted IS10 modules with unequal functional capacity.

variants.label: Tn9
variants.explanation: Direct IS1 repeats in classical Tn9; these are not host-derived TSDs.

exercise.question: Both Tn9 IS1 arrows point the same way. What follows?
options: Direct IS modules, not host TSDs
Tn9 must use the Tn5 pathway
exercise.explanation: Whole IS modules flank cargo. Their orientation does not establish a transposition mechanism.

check.question: Does resistance cargo itself encode the movement machinery in these examples?
options: No, that role is associated with the IS modules
check.explanation: Cargo and transposition functions are distinct; intact ends and functional machinery still matter.

variants.label: Insertion
variants.explanation: Run the existing conservative Tn5 model. Donor repair stays unresolved.

variants.label: Direct-repeat recombination
variants.explanation: Homology and direct orientation on one molecule are assumed. Retain the excised circle.

variants.label: Inverted-repeat recombination
variants.explanation: Homology and inverted orientation on one molecule are assumed.

variants.label: Unequal crossover
variants.explanation: Two sister substrates are required; inspect both reciprocal products.

exercise.question: Which event produces the modeled duplication?
exercise.explanation: Duplication requires the explicitly selected recombination substrates.

check.question: Where is the excised interval after direct-repeat recombination?
check.explanation: A deletion from the retained molecule need not destroy the excised DNA.

check2.question: Does inversion require a new transposition event here?

variants.label: Coding insertion
variants.explanation: Assume loss of enzyme function, no backup and growth requiring that pathway: phenotype likely altered.

variants.label: Intergenic insertion
variants.explanation: Assume no relevant function at this site under the selected condition: unchanged is plausible, not proven universally.

variants.label: Regulatory insertion
variants.explanation: Without promoter function and assay context, phenotype cannot be inferred.

variants.label: Condition changed
variants.explanation: Assume supplementation bypasses the lost pathway: growth may be unchanged even though molecular loss of function remains.

exercise.question: An insertion lies in a regulatory region, but the assay and promoter functions are unknown. Predict phenotype.
exercise.explanation: Position alone is insufficient.

check.question: Can supplementation mask a biosynthetic defect?
options: Yes, if the defined bypass assumptions hold
check.explanation: Phenotype can depend on environment.

check2.question: Does a coding insertion prove every measured trait changes?
check2.explanation: Molecular function and the assayed phenotype are separate levels.

variants.label: Promoter disruption
variants.explanation: Assume P is the sole functional promoter and is disabled: transcription from P is reduced.

variants.label: Outward promoter aligned
variants.explanation: Assume an active outward promoter faces an intact promoterless gene with no intervening terminator: transcription becomes possible. IS3 supplies a documented mobile-promoter example.

variants.label: Outward promoter reversed
variants.explanation: The promoter cannot directly drive rightward A transcription; without other promoter information total expression is undetermined.

variants.label: Operon termination
variants.explanation: Assume a functional terminator before B and no internal B promoter: downstream transcription is reduced (bacterial polarity).

variants.label: Read-through
variants.explanation: Assume P remains active, transcription passes through and B is intact: B transcription is permitted; protein abundance remains unknown.

exercise.question: A TE disrupts gene A but an independent promoter drives B. Must B transcription decrease?
exercise.explanation: Coding disruption is not the same as promoter loss or transcription termination.

check.question: Can a reversed outward promoter directly transcribe a rightward gene?
check.explanation: Transcription direction matters.

check2.question: What is needed to infer strong downstream transcriptional polarity here?
options: Effective termination and no bypass promoter
check2.explanation: Polarity depends on the specified bacterial context.

variants.label: Tn5 junction
variants.explanation: Inspect the existing Tn5 engine output and duplicated host interval.

variants.label: Tn3 junction
variants.explanation: Inspect the existing Tn3 cointegrate. Resolution is a separate operation.

variants.label: Non-universal outcome
variants.explanation: IS608 is a documented exception. No new IS608 engine is implemented.

exercise.question: Which features are host-derived?
exercise.explanation: The target interval is copied; the terminal recognition regions are element-derived.

check.question: Do two TSDs imply two element copies?
check.explanation: Tn5 retains one element overall despite two target repeats.

check2.question: Can Tn5’s 9 bp rule be assigned to every element?
check2.explanation: Tn3 has 5 bp in the selected system and IS608 has no TSD.

variants.label: Maize: Ds without Ac
variants.explanation: Assume no alternative compatible source: Ac-dependent transposition is not permitted.

variants.label: Maize: Ac supplied
variants.explanation: Under permissive host assumptions, the selected mobility gate is satisfied; an insertion is not guaranteed.

variants.label: Bacterial IS10: RNA-OUT
variants.explanation: Assume functional antisense pairing and no compensating protein supply: transposase production is reduced relative to the unpaired condition.

variants.label: Bacterial IS10: promoter inactive
variants.explanation: Assume no residual protein or alternative source: transposase availability gate is not met.

variants.label: Arabidopsis CACTA1: silenced
variants.explanation: Selected silenced CACTA1 context: mobility reduced relative to a released state. This is not bacterial regulation.

variants.label: Arabidopsis: ddm1 context
variants.explanation: CACTA1 mobilization is documented in ddm1 backgrounds, but a particular copy’s next event cannot be predicted from this condition alone.

exercise.question: RNA-OUT pairing is functional in bacterial IS10. What is the supported qualitative direction?
exercise.explanation: Antisense pairing inhibits translation in this documented system.

check.question: Does supplied Ac convert Ds into an autonomous element?
check.explanation: Protein supplied in trans does not change Ds coding capacity.

check2.question: Does ddm1 guarantee movement of every Arabidopsis TE?
check2.explanation: Host silencing effects depend on family, copy and cellular context.

variants.label: 1 · Identify bacterial DNA
variants.explanation: The chromosome is a cellular replicon; the plasmid is a separate replicon. Tn5 is a DNA element carried on a replicon, not a cell or an independently transferring plasmid.

variants.label: 2 · Within-cell movement
variants.explanation: The selected Tn5 event moves one element from a symbolic linear donor fragment to the circular target plasmid inside the donor cell. The fragment is not a simulated complete chromosome.

variants.label: 2 · Between-cell transfer
variants.explanation: Model a completed transfer with DNA synthesis and establishment assumed. The donor retains its plasmid; the recipient acquires a plasmid copy. This is not another transposition event.

variants.label: 2 · Nonconjugative plasmid
variants.explanation: This plasmid cannot self-transfer under these assumptions. Some nonconjugative plasmids are mobilizable with compatible helper functions; that is not modeled here.

variants.label: 3 · Resistance: starting state
blocks: linear donor fragment inside donor cell
variants.explanation: Classical Tn5 is a resistance-associated example. This curated symbolic fragment and conjugative target are not named experimental plasmids. Gene presence alone does not establish a resistance phenotype.

variants.label: 3 · Resistance: plasmid loading
variants.explanation: Calculate the existing Tn5 conservative insertion first. Transposition makes the target plasmid cargo-bearing without moving DNA between cells. Donor repair remains unresolved.

variants.label: 3 · Resistance: recipient acquisition
variants.explanation: After the separate transfer event, recipient DNA includes the determinant. Expression, host context and assay conditions remain unknown. Selection is not simulated; no treatment outcome is predicted.

variants.label: 4 · Tn7: glmS context
blocks: E. coli attTn7 region near glmS
variants.explanation: Native Tn7 TnsD (a TnsD/TniQ-family targeting factor) recognizes the glmS-associated context and recruits TnsC, which coordinates with TnsAB. This is the selected site-specific route; it is not TnsE recognition of replication structures.

variants.label: 4 · Tn7: transfer-related replication
variants.explanation: TnsE targets replication-associated structures, including conjugation-related DNA contexts. The context alone does not prove the attTn7 recognition route. It is not limited exclusively to plasmids.

variants.label: 4 · Tn7: mismatched route
variants.explanation: The supplied evidence supports TnsD recognition, not the selected TnsE route. Incompatible here means unsupported by this bounded context, not impossible in every biological circumstance.

variants.label: 5 · Integron cassette capture
variants.explanation: Compatible integrase and sites permit cassette capture by site-specific recombination. This is an explanatory diagram, not a computed recombination product; expression still depends on promoter and cassette context.

variants.label: 5 · Nested mobile DNA
variants.explanation: An IS primarily supplies transposition functions, a transposon may carry cargo, a plasmid is a replicon, and an integron captures/expresses cassettes. Nesting does not make these categories equivalent or make the plasmid conjugative.

exercise.question: Tn5 enters a plasmid, then the plasmid is conjugated into another cell. Which step is HGT?
options: Tn5 movement inside the donor alone
exercise.explanation: Molecular relocation and cellular dissemination are separate events.

check.question: Which target selector supports the established E. coli glmS-associated Tn7 route?
options: TnsD/TniQ-family factor with TnsC and TnsAB
check.explanation: TnsD directs attTn7 targeting; TnsE selects replication-associated contexts.

check2.question: An integron carrying a resistance cassette is on a plasmid. What follows?
options: It is itself a conjugative transposon
Capture is integrase-mediated; transfer and phenotype require separate evidence
check2.explanation: Cassette recombination, transposition, plasmid transfer and phenotypic selection are distinct.

variants.label: Complete protocol
variants.explanation: Every stage is present: membranes are opened, nucleases are held back, proteins and RNA are removed, and DNA is recovered from the cleared supernatant.

variants.label: No detergent
variants.explanation: Assume no other lysis method (such as grinding or bead beating). Many cells stay intact, and their DNA is discarded with the cell pellet.

variants.label: Protein removal skipped
blocks: no proteinase K, no salting out
variants.explanation: Proteins stay in solution and can come down with the DNA; any surviving nucleases can also act on it later.

variants.label: No EDTA, nucleases active
variants.explanation: Assume active cellular DNases and free divalent cations: DNA can be fragmented before the nucleases are digested or removed.

variants.label: No RNase A
variants.explanation: Alcohol precipitates RNA as well as DNA, so RNA co-purifies and inflates a concentration estimated from absorbance at 260 nm.

exercise.question: A lysate has been cleared of proteins and RNA. Which step recovers the DNA from this aqueous solution?
options: Alcohol precipitation in the presence of salt
exercise.explanation: Salt cations neutralize the phosphate backbone and alcohol lowers DNA solubility, so DNA comes out of solution and can be pelleted.

check.question: What does EDTA contribute to a lysis buffer?
options: It chelates Mg²⁺ so DNases are inhibited
check.explanation: DNases need divalent cations such as Mg²⁺. Binding them up protects the DNA; the detergent, not EDTA, opens membranes.

check2.question: Why is RNase A added when extracting genomic DNA?
options: RNA would also precipitate and contaminate the DNA
RNase A breaks open the nucleus
check2.explanation: Alcohol precipitation does not tell DNA from RNA, so RNA co-purifies unless it is degraded.

variants.label: Salt + 0.7 vol isopropanol
variants.explanation: Both requirements are met: the backbone charge is neutralized and the alcohol fraction is high enough. Room temperature limits salt co-precipitation.

variants.label: No salt added
variants.explanation: Assume the sample contains very little salt. Without cations to neutralize the backbone, DNA precipitates poorly.

variants.label: Too little alcohol
variants.explanation: The alcohol fraction is too low to drive DNA out of solution.

variants.label: Isopropanol on ice
blocks: chilled on ice for a long time
variants.explanation: DNA still precipitates, but cold isopropanol favours salt coming down with it.

variants.label: Ethanol instead
variants.explanation: Ethanol also works, needing roughly three times the alcohol volume; check the total still fits the tube.

exercise.question: You must precipitate DNA from 700 µL in a 1.5 mL tube. Which alcohol addition fits?
options: Either: the volume added makes no difference
exercise.explanation: 0.7 × 700 µL ≈ 490 µL, about 1.2 mL in total. 2.5 × 700 µL = 1750 µL would overflow the tube on its own.

check.question: Why is isopropanol precipitation usually done at room temperature?
options: DNA is unstable in the cold
check.explanation: Salts are less soluble in isopropanol, especially when it is cold, so they can pellet with the DNA.

check2.question: What role does the sodium acetate play?
options: Its Na⁺ ions neutralize the DNA phosphate backbone
check2.explanation: Neutralizing the negative charge lets DNA molecules aggregate once alcohol lowers the dielectric constant.

variants.label: 70% ethanol, brief air-dry
variants.explanation: Salt dissolves in the aqueous fraction, DNA stays pelleted, and only a little ethanol needs to evaporate.

variants.label: Wash with water
variants.explanation: DNA dissolves in water, so this “wash” pours the DNA away with the salt.

variants.label: Wash with 100% ethanol
variants.explanation: With almost no water present, salt is poorly removed. The DNA is kept, but purity barely improves.

variants.label: Wash skipped
variants.explanation: Salt and slow-evaporating isopropanol stay with the DNA.

variants.label: Not dried
variants.explanation: Residual ethanol can inhibit enzymes such as polymerases and make a loaded sample float out of the gel well.

variants.label: Over-dried
variants.explanation: An over-dried pellet, especially of large genomic DNA, can be slow and difficult to redissolve.

exercise.question: Why wash the pellet with 70% rather than 100% ethanol?
options: The water fraction dissolves salt while DNA stays insoluble
70% ethanol leaves no residue at all
exercise.explanation: The wash needs enough water to dissolve salt, but enough ethanol to keep DNA out of solution.

check.question: A sample floats out of the well when loaded on an agarose gel. What is the most likely cause?
check.explanation: Ethanol is less dense than the loading mixture, so leftover ethanol lifts the sample out of the well.

check2.question: Which reading most suggests the prep carried over something that absorbs near 230 nm?
check2.explanation: Guanidine salts from column kits, EDTA, phenol and carbohydrates absorb near 230 nm and lower A260/A230. The NaCl or sodium acetate left by a poor wash often leaves the ratio looking normal, so a good reading does not prove the salt is gone. A ratio flags a problem; it does not identify the contaminant.

variants.label: Your DNA from the wash
variants.explanation: Both ratios are in the usual range for pure DNA: 37.5 ng/µL, about 1.9 µg in 50 µL.

variants.label: Protein carried over
variants.explanation: Extra absorbance near 280 nm pulls A260/A280 well below about 1.8. Protein is the usual cause.

variants.label: RNase skipped
variants.explanation: Without RNase A, RNA precipitates with the DNA. RNA reads near 2.0 and also adds to A260.

variants.label: Carryover from the prep
variants.explanation: Something absorbing near 230 nm came along with the DNA. The ratio flags it but does not say what it is.

exercise.question: Your DNA reads A260 = 0.75 (10 mm path). What is its concentration?
exercise.explanation: For double-stranded DNA an A260 of 1.0 is about 50 ng/µL, so 0.75 × 50 = 37.5 ng/µL.

check.question: A sample’s A260/A280 is 1.60. What is the most likely explanation?
check.explanation: Protein absorbs near 280 nm and pulls the ratio below about 1.8. The ratio flags a problem; it does not prove what the contaminant is.

check2.question: RNase A was skipped and A260/A280 reads 2.05. What else is wrong with this reading?
options: The A260 concentration overestimates the DNA
The ratio proves the sample is pure
check2.explanation: RNA also absorbs at 260 nm, so it inflates the concentration calculated from A260.

variants.label: Standard set-up
variants.explanation: Both primers bind their own sites and every product is a new template: one band of the expected size.

variants.label: Primers pointing away
variants.explanation: Primers that point away from each other never define a region between them, so nothing is amplified.

variants.label: Annealing at 72 °C
variants.explanation: Well above their melting temperature, the primers barely stay bound, so little or nothing is copied.

variants.label: Annealing at 45 °C
variants.explanation: Far below the melting temperature, primers also bind partly matching sites and make extra products.

variants.label: Only 10 cycles
variants.explanation: The right product, but 2¹⁰ is only about a thousand-fold: too little to see clearly.

exercise.question: Starting from about 1,100 template copies, roughly how many copies do 10 ideal cycles give?

check.question: Why does the target roughly double every cycle?
options: Each strand of every duplex is a template for a new strand
The polymerase copies each strand twice
check.explanation: After denaturation both strands are templates, and each new strand carries the other primer’s site.

check2.question: You anneal far above the primers’ melting temperature. Predict the result.
check2.explanation: Above their Tm the primers do not stay bound long enough to be extended.

variants.label: 1% gel, wells at −
variants.explanation: DNA moves toward the anode and separates by size; the product sits between 800 and 900 bp.

variants.label: Electrodes reversed
variants.explanation: DNA still moves toward the positive electrode, which is now behind the wells, so it leaves the gel into the buffer.
variants.outcome: DNA runs out of the gel

variants.label: Ethanol left in the sample
variants.explanation: Residual ethanol makes the sample less dense than the loading mixture, so it floats up out of the well.

variants.label: Run stopped early
variants.explanation: The fragments have barely entered the gel, so neighbouring sizes have not separated yet.

exercise.question: The band sits between the 800 and 900 bp ladder bands, about halfway on the log scale. What is the best estimate?
exercise.explanation: Halfway on a log scale between 800 and 900 is √(800 × 900) ≈ 849 bp.

check.question: Which way do DNA fragments move in the gel?
check.explanation: The phosphate backbone is negatively charged, so DNA moves toward the anode.

check2.question: Why plot the ladder as log(size) against distance?
options: Distance falls roughly linearly with log(size) over the gel’s range
check2.explanation: Distance travelled falls roughly linearly as log(size) rises, so a log scale turns the ladder into a straight line to read from.

variants.label: EcoRI
variants.explanation: One cut, 300 bp from one end, of a linear 850 bp molecule: two pieces.

variants.label: BamHI
variants.explanation: The amplicon has no BamHI site, so the enzyme has nothing to cut.

variants.label: EcoRI + HindIII
variants.explanation: Two cuts in a linear molecule give three pieces: 300, 400 and 150 bp.

variants.label: EcoRI, short incubation
variants.explanation: Some molecules are still uncut, so an 850 bp band remains beside 550 and 300 bp.

exercise.question: EcoRI cuts the 850 bp product once, 300 bp from one end. Which bands do you expect?
exercise.explanation: 850 − 300 = 550, so the cut leaves 300 and 550 bp pieces.

check.question: A linear DNA has two sites for an enzyme. How many fragments does a complete digest give?
check.explanation: n cuts in a linear molecule give n + 1 pieces. A circle with two sites would give two.

check2.question: After an EcoRI digest you see bands at 850, 550 and 300 bp. What is most likely?
check2.explanation: The 850 bp band is uncut product: some molecules were never cut.

questions.question: Ds moves when Ac protein is supplied. What is Ds?
questions.explanation: Supplying protein changes mobility conditions, not the genetic capacity encoded by Ds.

questions.question: Remove Ac and every other compatible transposase source. Predict Ds mobility.
questions.explanation: The selected Ds cannot encode functional transposase.

questions.question: Which regions move as part of this element?
questions.explanation: TIRs lie inside element boundaries; TSDs lie outside.

questions.question: Two flanking direct host repeats demonstrate what?
questions.explanation: Count complete elements independently of the target repeats.

questions.question: An element uses RNA followed by reverse transcription. Classify it.
options: Class II because its product is DNA
questions.explanation: The intermediate and reverse-transcription step identify Class I.

questions.question: One circle contains both backbones and two direct Tn3 copies. What occurred?
questions.explanation: The selected replicative transition joins backbones and increases copy number.

questions.question: After conservative Tn5 transposition, how many element copies remain overall?
options: One — the element moves from donor to target.
Two — a new copy is made while the donor copy remains.
questions.explanation: Conservative movement relocates the original element. The two new flanking repeats are host-derived TSDs; they are not additional element copies.

questions.question: What distinguishes the completed Tn3 cointegrate from the initial replicons?
options: Two separate circles with one copy overall.
One circle containing both backbones and two directly oriented Tn3 copies.
One circle with one Tn3 and no donor backbone.
questions.explanation: Replicative transposition adds a second Tn3 copy and joins donor and target into one circular cointegrate.

questions.question: What should TnpR-mediated resolution do to the two Tn3 copies?
options: Remove one copy to restore a total of one.
Separate the replicon structures while preserving two copies overall.
questions.explanation: Recombination at the internal res sites partitions the cointegrate into two replicon products. Each retains one recombinant Tn3. Physical decatenation is not modeled.

questions.question: Which region directly supplies movement machinery?
questions.explanation: Resistance cargo has a different function from transposition genes.

questions.question: Both Tn9 IS1 arrows point the same way. What follows?
options: Direct IS modules, not host TSDs
Tn9 must use the Tn5 pathway
questions.explanation: Whole IS modules flank cargo. Their orientation does not establish a transposition mechanism.

questions.question: Which event produces the modeled duplication?
questions.explanation: Duplication requires the explicitly selected recombination substrates.

questions.question: Does inversion require a new transposition event here?
questions.explanation: This model labels recombination separately.

questions.question: An insertion lies in a regulatory region, but the assay and promoter functions are unknown. Predict phenotype.
questions.explanation: Position alone is insufficient.

questions.question: Does a coding insertion prove every measured trait changes?
questions.explanation: Molecular function and the assayed phenotype are separate levels.

questions.question: A TE disrupts gene A but an independent promoter drives B. Must B transcription decrease?
questions.explanation: Coding disruption is not the same as promoter loss or transcription termination.

questions.question: What is needed to infer strong downstream transcriptional polarity here?
options: Effective termination and no bypass promoter
questions.explanation: Polarity depends on the specified bacterial context.

questions.question: Which features are host-derived?
questions.explanation: The target interval is copied; the terminal recognition regions are element-derived.

questions.question: Can Tn5’s 9 bp rule be assigned to every element?
questions.explanation: Tn3 has 5 bp in the selected system and IS608 has no TSD.

questions.question: Do two TSDs imply two element copies?
questions.explanation: Tn5 retains one element overall despite two target repeats.

questions.question: RNA-OUT pairing is functional in bacterial IS10. What is the supported qualitative direction?
questions.explanation: Antisense pairing inhibits translation in this documented system.

questions.question: Does ddm1 guarantee movement of every Arabidopsis TE?
questions.explanation: Host silencing effects depend on family, copy and cellular context.

questions.question: Tn5 enters a plasmid, then the plasmid is conjugated into another cell. Which step is HGT?
options: Tn5 movement inside the donor alone
questions.explanation: Molecular relocation and cellular dissemination are separate events.

questions.question: An integron carrying a resistance cassette is on a plasmid. What follows?
options: It is itself a conjugative transposon
Capture is integrase-mediated; transfer and phenotype require separate evidence
questions.explanation: Cassette recombination, transposition, plasmid transfer and phenotypic selection are distinct.

questions.question: Which target selector supports the established E. coli glmS-associated Tn7 route?
options: TnsD/TniQ-family factor with TnsC and TnsAB
questions.explanation: TnsD directs attTn7 targeting; TnsE selects replication-associated contexts.
